4-axis-Cost-Benefit.card_intro: Connect total benefit, total cost, net benefit, marginal benefit and marginal cost across four linked panels.
4-axis-Cost-Benefit.card_prompt: Move the quantity slider and identify the point at which net benefit is maximised.
4-axis-Cost-Benefit.intro_html:
This graph brings the main pieces of cost-benefit analysis onto one screen. The same quantity appears in every panel, so moving the slider lets you compare total benefit, total cost and net benefit with their marginal counterparts.

The central question is not simply whether benefit is large. It is whether one more unit adds more benefit than cost.
4-axis-Cost-Benefit.full_html:
Net benefit is the difference between total benefit and total cost:

\[NB(q)=B(q)-C(q).\]

Differentiating gives the slope of net benefit:

\[NB'(q)=MB(q)-MC(q).\]

If \(MB(q)>MC(q)\), increasing quantity raises net benefit. If \(MB(q)<MC(q)\), the next unit adds more cost than benefit, so net benefit falls. At an interior maximum,

\[NB'(q^{*})=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad MB(q^{*})=MC(q^{*}).\]

The equality is a marginal condition, not a claim that total benefit equals total cost. Check the total curves as well: at the optimum, the vertical gap \(B(q)-C(q)\) is largest. If the marginal curves do not cross within the feasible range, compare the boundary quantities.

Elasticity-Flexible-Demand.card_intro: Use a power demand curve to see why its price elasticity is constant even as price and quantity change.
Elasticity-Flexible-Demand.card_prompt: Move the price marker, then change the exponent and compare the elasticity readout.
Elasticity-Flexible-Demand.intro_html: The demand function in this graph is \(Q_D(p)=Ap^{-B}\), with \(A>0\) and \(B>0\). The marker shows a price-quantity pair while the elasticity panel reports the local percentage response.
Elasticity-Flexible-Demand.full_html:
Point price elasticity is

\[E_D(p)=Q_D'(p)\frac{p}{Q_D(p)}.\]

For the power demand function, \(Q_D'(p)=-ABp^{-B-1}\), so

\[E_D(p)=-B.\]

That is the useful feature of this example: moving along the curve changes price, quantity and slope, but it does not change elasticity. The scale parameter \(A\) shifts the quantity demanded at every price; the exponent \(B\) controls the absolute elasticity. Demand is elastic when \(B>1\), unit elastic when \(B=1\), and inelastic when \(0<B<1\).

Do not infer elasticity from steepness alone. The elasticity formula combines slope with the price-to-quantity ratio, which is why curves with changing slopes can still have constant elasticity.

Elasticity-Staircase-Demand.card_intro: Explore elasticity when demand changes in discrete jumps rather than along a smooth curve.
Elasticity-Staircase-Demand.card_prompt: Move price through a jump and compare the economic change with the local derivative-based measure.
Elasticity-Staircase-Demand.intro_html:
This graph uses a three-step demand schedule. Over a range of prices, quantity demanded may remain unchanged; at a threshold price, it jumps to another level.

The example is useful because it shows where the familiar point-elasticity formula needs care.
Elasticity-Staircase-Demand.full_html:
For a differentiable demand curve, point elasticity is \(E_D(p)=Q_D'(p)p/Q_D(p)\). On a flat portion of the staircase as a function of price, quantity is locally constant, so the local response is zero. At a jump price, however, the derivative does not exist and point elasticity is not defined.

This does not mean the jump has no economic importance. It means a derivative is the wrong summary at that point. For a finite movement from \((p_1,Q_1)\) to \((p_2,Q_2)\), use a discrete or midpoint elasticity:

\[E_D^{mid}=\frac{(Q_2-Q_1)/[(Q_1+Q_2)/2]}{(p_2-p_1)/[(p_1+p_2)/2]}.\]

The graph therefore separates two ideas: local elasticity within a price interval and the finite response when a threshold is crossed.

Market-interventions-revised.card_intro: Compare taxes, subsidies, price floors, price support and quantity restrictions in one supply-and-demand market.
Market-interventions-revised.card_prompt: Select a policy, set the desired market price and trace the changes in price, quantity, surplus and government activity.
Market-interventions-revised.intro_html:
This graph compares several market interventions against the competitive benchmark. Start with no intervention, then change the policy type, the side of the market where relevant, and the target price.

Taxes, subsidies, price floors, government price support and quotas are core policies. Voluntary reduction is included as an extension for comparison.
Market-interventions-revised.full_html:
Without intervention, equilibrium occurs where demand equals supply. A per-unit tax creates a wedge between the price paid by buyers and the price received by sellers; who remits the tax is not the same as who bears its economic burden. A subsidy creates the opposite wedge and expands trade.

A binding price floor sets a legal minimum above equilibrium. If the government does not purchase the surplus, the quantity traded is limited by demand. With price support, government purchases can maintain the target price, but the fiscal cost and surplus production must be counted.

A quota restricts quantity directly. When the restriction binds, the gap between willingness to pay and marginal cost becomes a quota rent. Its distribution depends on who owns the quota rights. Voluntary reduction can mimic a quantity restriction only if participants actually coordinate on the lower quantity; it is less central because the enforcement and incentive problem is outside this partial-equilibrium picture.

For every policy, identify four objects before comparing welfare: the buyer price, the seller price, the quantity traded, and any government revenue or expenditure. A policy that raises the observed market price need not raise total surplus.

Lectorial.card_intro: Practise turning total benefit and total cost functions into a net-benefit maximisation problem.
Lectorial.card_prompt: Find the quantity that maximises net benefit, then verify it using both total and marginal curves.
Lectorial.intro_html: The graph uses \(B(H)=654H-40H^2\) and \(C(H)=110H+40H^2\). Use the sliders and curves to form a prediction before opening the solution.
Lectorial.full_html: Calculate net benefit, marginal benefit and marginal cost. The optimum is where the marginal gain from a little more \(H\) is just offset by its marginal cost, provided the candidate is feasible and is a maximum.
Lectorial.answer_html:
Net benefit is

\[NB(H)=B(H)-C(H)=544H-80H^2.\]

The marginal functions are

\[MB(H)=654-80H,\qquad MC(H)=110+80H.\]

Set \(MB(H)=MC(H)\):

\[654-80H=110+80H\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H^{*}=3.4.\]

Because \(NB''(H)=-160<0\), this stationary point is a maximum. On the total-curves panel, the vertical gap between benefit and cost is largest at \(H=3.4\).

Max.card_intro: Minimise total loss by balancing the benefit of inspection against its direct cost.
Max.card_prompt: Derive the optimal inspection level and explain why the same point can be described using marginal benefit and marginal cost.
Max.intro_html: Inspection reduces harm according to \(H(x)=a/(x+1)\), while inspection itself costs \(C(x)=bx\). The decision can be written either as minimising total loss \(H(x)+C(x)\) or maximising avoided harm net of inspection cost.
Max.full_html: The benefit of inspection is the harm avoided relative to no inspection: \(B(x)=H(0)-H(x)\). This reframing makes the marginal rule transparent but does not change the optimal choice.
Max.answer_html:
Total loss is

\[L(x)=\frac{a}{x+1}+bx.\]

For an interior solution,

\[L'(x)=-\frac{a}{(x+1)^2}+b=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{a}{b}}-1.\]

Equivalently, the marginal benefit of inspection is \(a/(x+1)^2\) and the marginal cost is \(b\). With the graph's default values \(a=32\) and \(b=2\), \(x^{*}=3\). Since \(L''(x)=2a/(x+1)^3>0\), this is a minimum. If \(a\le b\), the interior formula is non-positive and the constrained optimum is the corner \(x^{*}=0\).

W1Quiz.card_intro: Review partial derivatives, a nonlinear system and differentiation of a logarithmic function used in later consumer-choice problems.
W1Quiz.card_prompt: Work through all parts without revealing the answer folders, then use the graph to check your calculations.
W1Quiz.intro_html: This short mathematical review has three parts: evaluate a function and its partial derivatives; solve a nonlinear system subject to positive quantities; and evaluate and differentiate a logarithmic function.
W1Quiz.full_html: Keep the economic domain in view. Algebra can produce candidates that are undefined or irrelevant when quantities must be positive.
W1Quiz.answer_html:
For \(f(x,y)=x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}\),

\[f_x=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}y^{\beta},\qquad f_y=\beta x^{\alpha}y^{\beta-1}.\]

With \(\alpha=1\), \(\beta=2\) and \((x,y)=(2,2)\), the values are \(f=8\), \(f_x=4\) and \(f_y=8\).

For the system \(y^2/x^3=1/4\) and \(4x+5y=36\), positivity gives \(y=\tfrac12x^{3/2}\). Substitution into the linear equation yields the positive solution \((x,y)=(4,4)\). Check both original equations rather than relying only on the transformed system.

For \(g(x)=5\ln x\),

\[g(10)=5\ln(10)\approx11.513,\qquad g'(x)=\frac{5}{x},\qquad g'(10)=0.5.\]

Elasticity.card_intro: Connect slope, percentage responsiveness and total movement along linear demand and supply curves.
Elasticity.card_prompt: Move the price marker from one intercept to the other and track how elasticity changes even though slope is constant.
Elasticity.intro_html: This graph starts with linear demand \(Q_D(p)=A-Bp\) and then adds supply. The derivative is constant, but elasticity is not, because elasticity measures percentage rather than unit changes.
Elasticity.full_html:
Demand elasticity is

\[E_D(p)=Q_D'(p)\frac{p}{Q_D(p)}=-B\frac{p}{A-Bp}.\]

Near the quantity intercept, price is small relative to quantity and demand is inelastic. Moving upward along the same straight line raises the absolute elasticity; at the midpoint it is unit elastic, and near the choke price it becomes very large. This is why “steep” and “inelastic” are not interchangeable.

For a finite price change, the midpoint method uses average price and average quantity, avoiding a different percentage depending on the direction of comparison. The supply panel applies the same logic with \(E_S(p)=Q_S'(p)p/Q_S(p)\); supply elasticity is normally positive while demand elasticity is negative, so demand is often discussed in absolute value.

Consumers-Problem.card_intro: Build the consumer's problem from the budget set, preferences and the highest attainable indifference curve.
Consumers-Problem.card_prompt: Switch preference types and test when tangency, a corner or a kink determines the optimum.
Consumers-Problem.intro_html: The consumer chooses a feasible bundle to maximise utility. The graph lets you move a bundle, show its upper contour set and indifference curve, and compare several preference specifications with the budget set.
Consumers-Problem.full_html:
The budget set is \(p_xx+p_yy\le I\). With monotonic preferences, the optimum lies on the budget line. At a smooth interior optimum, the indifference curve is tangent to that line:

\[MRS_{xy}=\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}=\frac{p_x}{p_y}.\]

The equality says the consumer's willingness to trade \(y\) for \(x\) matches the market trade-off. It is not a universal recipe. Perfect substitutes can produce a corner, perfect complements are optimised at a kink, and some parameter values make a boundary bundle optimal.

Use the utility selector to compare Cobb-Douglas, quasilinear, power, CES, perfect-complements and perfect-substitutes preferences. When a control changes, first identify whether it changes the feasible set or preferences; only then interpret the movement in the chosen bundle.

Indifference-curve.card_intro: Inspect indifference curves and the marginal rate of substitution for Cobb-Douglas and an alternative utility specification.
Indifference-curve.card_prompt: Move the reference bundle and compare the local slope of its indifference curve across the two utility types.
Indifference-curve.intro_html: An indifference curve collects all bundles that deliver the same utility. Its slope is determined by the marginal rate of substitution, not by the numerical level assigned to utility.
Indifference-curve.full_html:
For a differentiable utility function, holding utility constant gives

\[\frac{dy}{dx}\bigg|_{u=\bar u}=-\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}=-MRS_{xy}.\]

For Cobb-Douglas utility, the curves are smooth, downward sloping and convex under the usual positive parameters. Moving the reference bundle changes the utility level and therefore selects a different curve.

The second specification is labelled as an inferior-good example, but an indifference curve by itself does not prove that a good is inferior. Inferiority is a property of demand: after solving the constrained choice problem, demand for that good must fall when income rises, holding prices fixed. The separate Week 3 graph performs that income comparison and also reveals why corner and global-optimum checks matter.

Utility-Max.card_intro: View Cobb-Douglas utility as a three-dimensional surface and the budget constraint as a feasible slice.
Utility-Max.card_prompt: Rotate the graph, change prices or income and locate the highest utility reached along the budget line.
Utility-Max.intro_html: This optional 3D view adds height to the usual indifference-curve diagram: each point \((x,y)\) has height \(u(x,y)\). The budget line restricts the consumer to a path across the surface.
Utility-Max.full_html:
Maximising utility means finding the highest point on that feasible path. In a two-dimensional diagram, the same calculation appears as the highest attainable indifference curve. For Cobb-Douglas utility \(u=x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}\), an interior solution satisfies

\[\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}=\frac{p_x}{p_y}.\]

The 3D view is especially helpful for seeing that the first-order condition is about the slope along the constraint. It is not necessary for routine calculation, but it connects the algebra, the indifference map and the underlying utility surface.

Discrete-Demand-Supply.card_intro: Construct market demand and supply from individual bids and asks, producing staircase curves and discrete trades.
Discrete-Demand-Supply.card_prompt: Change the number of traders or apply a unit tax, then identify which marginal trades still create surplus.
Discrete-Demand-Supply.intro_html: Each buyer submits a willingness to pay and each seller submits a willingness to accept. Sorting these values creates staircase demand and supply schedules rather than smooth curves.
Discrete-Demand-Supply.full_html:
A trade creates gains when the buyer's willingness to pay is at least the seller's opportunity cost. Starting with the highest bid and lowest ask, continue trading while

\[WTP_k\ge WTA_k.\]

With discrete traders, the efficient quantity is an integer and the competitive price may be an interval rather than a unique number. Total surplus is the sum of \(WTP_k-WTA_k\) over completed trades.

A unit tax can be represented by lowering buyers' net bids or raising sellers' effective asks. Either representation creates the same wedge and can eliminate marginal trades. Changing the number of bids and asks shows how a larger market can make the staircase appear smoother; that comparison is useful, but the essential lesson is horizontal aggregation and the surplus test for each trade.

Budget-Line-With-Complex-Pricing.card_intro: Work with a kinked budget line created by two marginal prices for the same good.
Budget-Line-With-Complex-Pricing.card_prompt: Derive the budget line, solve within each pricing tier and compare the candidates with the kink.
Budget-Line-With-Complex-Pricing.intro_html: The first \(C\) units of \(x\) cost \(p_{1x}\) each and later units cost \(p_{2x}\) each. Because the marginal price changes at \(x=C\), the budget line has a kink.
Budget-Line-With-Complex-Pricing.full_html: A single average price can describe total expenditure, but it does not remove the need to respect the two marginal-price regions when optimising. Generate a candidate for each smooth segment, include the kink and feasible corners, then compare utility.
Budget-Line-With-Complex-Pricing.answer_html:
Total expenditure on \(x\) is

\[p_{1x}\min\{C,x\}+p_{2x}\max\{x-C,0\}.\]

Hence the budget constraint is this expression plus \(p_yy=I\). Below the threshold, solve using price \(p_{1x}\). Above it, the constraint can be rewritten as

\[p_{2x}x+p_yy=I-(p_{1x}-p_{2x})C.\]

For the displayed power utility \(u=x^r y^{\beta}\), the first-tier interior candidate is

\[x_1=\frac{r}{r+\beta}\frac{I}{p_{1x}}.\]

With the default settings, \(x_1\approx13.99<C=20\), so it is valid and the second tier is not reached. In other settings, discard candidates outside their own tier, calculate the valid second-tier candidate using the adjusted income, and compare both with \(x=C\) and the feasible corners. The common mistake is to use the cheaper later-unit price for every unit.

Consumers-Problem-Lecture-Example.card_intro: Solve the lecture consumer-choice example using both Cobb-Douglas demand and the tangency condition.
Consumers-Problem-Lecture-Example.card_prompt: Calculate the optimal bundle, place it on the graph and verify that it exhausts the budget.
Consumers-Problem-Lecture-Example.intro_html: The graph uses prices \(p_x=9\), \(p_y=12\), income \(I=69\) and utility proportional to \(x^{1/3}y\).
Consumers-Problem-Lecture-Example.full_html: Use the budget equation and either Cobb-Douglas expenditure shares or \(MRS=p_x/p_y\). A numerical bundle is not enough: check feasibility and explain why it is the highest attainable indifference curve.
Consumers-Problem-Lecture-Example.answer_html:
For \(u=x^{1/3}y\), the exponents are \(1/3\) and \(1\). The corresponding expenditure shares are \(1/4\) on \(x\) and \(3/4\) on \(y\). Therefore

\[x^{*}=\frac{1}{4}\frac{69}{9}=\frac{23}{12}\approx1.917,\qquad y^{*}=\frac{3}{4}\frac{69}{12}=\frac{69}{16}=4.3125.\]

The budget check is \(9x^{*}+12y^{*}=69\). Since both quantities are positive and Cobb-Douglas preferences are strictly convex, this interior tangency is the unique optimum.

Inferior-Good.card_intro: See how a non-convex utility example can generate an income range in which demand for good x falls as income rises.
Inferior-Good.card_prompt: Increase income slowly, track every stationary bundle and compare each one with the x-axis corner before naming the optimum.
Inferior-Good.intro_html: The graph uses \(u(x,y)=a\ln x+y^2/2\) with budget \(p_xx+p_yy\le I\). It is deliberately tricky: the utility function is not globally concave, so a first-order condition alone does not identify the global optimum.
Inferior-Good.full_html:
At an interior stationary bundle,

\[\frac{a}{xy}=\frac{p_x}{p_y},\qquad p_xx+p_yy=I.\]

Eliminating \(x\) gives

\[y^2-\frac{I}{p_y}y+a=0.\]

Real stationary bundles exist only when \((I/p_y)^2-4a\ge0\). Of the two roots, the smaller-​\(y\) root is a local minimum along the budget line; the larger-​\(y\) root can be a local maximum. Even then, it must be compared with the feasible corner \((I/p_x,0)\).

With the default settings, the corner delivers higher utility than either stationary bundle. Once the interior maximum becomes globally preferred, its first-order condition implies \(x=ap_y/(p_xy)\). As income raises the chosen \(y\), chosen \(x\) falls: good \(x\) is inferior on that branch. Inferiority is therefore a statement about the income response of Marshallian demand, not about the visual shape of one indifference curve.

Perfect-Complements.card_intro: Optimise L-shaped preferences when goods are useful only in a fixed proportion.
Perfect-Complements.card_prompt: Change prices and income, then check why the chosen bundle remains on the kink ray rather than satisfying a smooth tangency.
Perfect-Complements.intro_html: With perfect complements, utility is \(u(x,y)=\min\{ax,by\}\). Extra units of only one good do not raise utility, so efficient bundles lie where the two components are balanced.
Perfect-Complements.full_html:
The kink condition is \(ax=by\). Combining it with the binding budget \(p_xx+p_yy=I\) gives

\[x^{*}=\frac{bI}{bp_x+ap_y},\qquad y^{*}=\frac{aI}{bp_x+ap_y}.\]

A smooth tangency condition is not available at the kink because the indifference curve has no single slope there. Price changes alter how much of the fixed-proportion bundle the consumer can afford, but they do not induce substitution away from the required proportion. This is the limiting case of zero substitutability.

Quasi-Linear-Optimization.card_intro: Solve a quasilinear consumer problem and isolate the special income effect implied by its demand functions.
Quasi-Linear-Optimization.card_prompt: Change income and verify which good's demand stays fixed at an interior solution.
Quasi-Linear-Optimization.intro_html: The graph uses \(u(x,y)=x+\sqrt y\) and budget \(p_xx+p_yy=I\). Utility is linear in \(x\) but curved in \(y\).
Quasi-Linear-Optimization.full_html:
At an interior optimum,

\[\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}=2\sqrt y=\frac{p_x}{p_y}.\]

Therefore

\[y^{*}=\left(\frac{p_x}{2p_y}\right)^2,\qquad x^{*}=\frac{I}{p_x}-\frac{p_x}{4p_y}.\]

Demand for \(y\) is independent of income at the interior solution, while additional income is spent on \(x\). This does not mean income never matters: if income is too low to afford the interior \(y^{*}\), the solution moves to a corner and the interior formulas no longer apply.

Revealed-Preference.card_intro: Infer preference comparisons from observed choices and the budget sets that made alternatives affordable.
Revealed-Preference.card_prompt: Step through the observations and shade only the bundles whose ranking is justified by actual affordability.
Revealed-Preference.intro_html: Revealed preference uses choice rather than a stated utility function. If bundle \(A\) is chosen when bundle \(B\) was affordable, then \(A\) is directly revealed weakly preferred to \(B\).
Revealed-Preference.full_html:
The budget line matters as much as the chosen point. A bundle outside the observed budget set was not available, so the observation says nothing about how it compares with the choice.

Chains of justified comparisons produce indirect revealed preference. If \(A\) is revealed preferred to \(B\) and \(B\) to \(C\), then the data support ranking \(A\) above \(C\). A revealed-preference violation occurs when later behaviour contradicts such a ranking under the relevant affordability conditions. Use the rollout control to separate observed facts from conclusions that require transitivity.

Utility-Max-CES.card_intro: Use CES preferences to vary substitutability continuously between near-complements and near-substitutes.
Utility-Max-CES.card_prompt: Move the curvature parameter and compare the indifference curves, optimal bundle and demand response.
Utility-Max-CES.intro_html: The graph uses a constant-elasticity-of-substitution utility function of the form \(u=[(ax)^r+(by)^r]^{1/r}\). The curvature parameter \(r\) changes how readily the consumer substitutes between goods.
Utility-Max-CES.full_html:
For the standard CES form, the elasticity of substitution is \(\sigma=1/(1-r)\). As \(r\) approaches one, preferences approach perfect substitutes; as \(r\) becomes very negative, they approach perfect complements. Intermediate values produce smooth, convex indifference curves.

At an interior optimum, the marginal-rate-of-substitution condition matches the price ratio. Changing \(r\) changes the curvature of the indifference curves and therefore the strength of the substitution response to a relative-price change. Compare the CES solution with the displayed perfect-complements benchmark, and remember that limiting cases can replace a smooth tangency with a corner or kink.

Sales-vs-Income-Tax.card_intro: Compare a tax on one good with an income tax that raises the same revenue, then separate substitution and income effects.
Sales-vs-Income-Tax.card_prompt: Set a sales tax, match its revenue with an income tax and compare the resulting budget lines and chosen bundles.
Sales-vs-Income-Tax.intro_html: A sales tax on one good changes its relative price and rotates the budget line. An income tax reduces purchasing power while leaving the relative-price slope unchanged. Matching revenue makes their behavioural difference visible.
Sales-vs-Income-Tax.full_html:
The sales tax combines a substitution effect with an income effect: the taxed good becomes relatively more expensive and real purchasing power falls. A revenue-equivalent income tax creates the income effect without the same relative-price distortion. In this standard consumer model, the income tax therefore generally allows at least as much utility as the commodity tax for the same revenue, although administrative and distributional considerations are outside the graph.

The compensation controls illustrate two different benchmarks. Hicksian compensation restores the original utility level. Slutsky compensation gives enough income to make the original bundle affordable at new prices. They are distinct for a finite price change but coincide to first order for a very small change. Label the benchmark before interpreting an “income effect.”

Aggregate-Demand.card_intro: Build market demand by horizontally adding the quantities demanded by individual consumers at each price.
Aggregate-Demand.card_prompt: Change the number of consumers and verify how the aggregate curve shifts while individual demand stays fixed.
Aggregate-Demand.intro_html: The baseline individual demand is \(q_i(p)=10-p\) over the range where quantity is non-negative. With identical consumers, market demand is the horizontal sum of their quantities.
Aggregate-Demand.full_html:
For \(N\) identical active consumers,

\[Q_D(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_i(p)=N(10-p).\]

Horizontal addition means holding price fixed and adding quantities; it does not mean adding prices vertically. When consumers have different demand functions or choke prices, include only those with positive demand at the price being considered. This can create kinks in aggregate demand as consumers enter or leave the market.

Consumers-Problem-HW.card_intro: Compare no tax, a sales tax on good 2 and an income tax that raises the same revenue for a Cobb-Douglas consumer.
Consumers-Problem-HW.card_prompt: Calculate all three bundles and explain which tax changes relative prices.
Consumers-Problem-HW.intro_html: The default problem uses \(p_1=10\), \(p_2=5\), \(I=702\) and equal Cobb-Douglas weights. A sales tax of rate \(r\) applies to good 2; the income-tax rate is chosen to collect the same revenue.
Consumers-Problem-HW.full_html: Use Cobb-Douglas expenditure shares first, then match tax revenue. Distinguish the statutory tax rate from the economic change in the consumer's budget set.
Consumers-Problem-HW.answer_html:
With \(\alpha=\beta=1\), the untaxed consumer spends one half of income on each good:

\[(x_0,y_0)=\left(\frac{I}{2p_1},\frac{I}{2p_2}\right)=(35.1,70.2).\]

Under the sales tax, the effective price of good 2 is \(p_2(1+r)\). With \(r=0.52\),

\[(x_r,y_r)=\left(35.1,\frac{702}{2\cdot5\cdot1.52}\right)\approx(35.1,46.184).\]

Sales-tax revenue is \(p_2r y_r\). The revenue-equivalent income-tax rate is therefore

\[t=\frac{p_2r y_r}{I}\approx0.171053.\]

The income-tax bundle is

\[(x_t,y_t)=\left(\frac{I(1-t)}{2p_1},\frac{I(1-t)}{2p_2}\right)\approx(29.096,58.192).\]

The sales tax leaves spending on good 1 unchanged for this Cobb-Douglas case but distorts the relative price; the income tax reduces both quantities proportionally. Compare utility, not just one coordinate, when deciding which bundle the consumer prefers.

Curves&Demand.card_intro: Link optimal choices to price-consumption curves, income-consumption curves, ordinary demand and Engel curves.
Curves&Demand.card_prompt: Switch among the three utility types and compare own-price, cross-price and income responses.
Curves&Demand.intro_html: This multi-panel graph turns repeated solutions of the consumer's problem into demand relationships. Each curve answers a different comparative-statics question, so identify which variable changes and which are held fixed.
Curves&Demand.full_html:
A price-consumption curve traces optimal bundles as one price changes; projecting the relevant coordinate against that price gives an ordinary demand curve. An income-consumption curve traces optima as income changes; projecting quantity against income gives an Engel curve.

The selector compares an independent-goods Cobb-Douglas case with specifications designed to show gross substitutes and gross complements. “Gross” refers to the total Marshallian response, which combines substitution and income effects. A positive cross-price response identifies gross substitutes, while a negative one identifies gross complements. Do not infer the sign from the shape of a single indifference curve without solving the demand response.

Curves-Expansion-Demand.card_intro: Trace how optimal consumption expands with income and changes with prices, then read demand and Engel curves from those choices.
Curves-Expansion-Demand.card_prompt: Move one price or income at a time and identify the corresponding consumption path before reading the projected curve.
Curves-Expansion-Demand.intro_html: The graph combines the budget line, indifference curves, demand functions and optimal bundle with price- and income-consumption paths. It is a map from repeated optimisation problems to observable demand.
Curves-Expansion-Demand.full_html:
When income changes with prices fixed, the optimum traces an income-expansion path. The associated quantity-income relationship is an Engel curve and reveals whether a good is normal or inferior over the displayed range. When one price changes, the optimum traces a price-consumption curve; the associated price-quantity relationship is ordinary demand.

Ordinary demand contains both substitution and income effects. Cross-price movements may therefore reveal gross substitution or gross complementarity even when the compensated substitution effect has a clearer sign. Keep the experiment controlled: change one slider, name what is fixed, and then interpret the path.

Ex-2023-Q3.card_intro: Work through an intertemporal consumer-choice exam example with a large interest-rate change and a compensated decomposition.
Ex-2023-Q3.card_prompt: Calculate the initial and new bundles, then adjust the transfer before reading the substitution and income effects.
Ex-2023-Q3.intro_html: Despite an outdated note inside the graph, its equations describe intertemporal consumption. Present and future resources are \(M_1=M_2=105\), prices are \(p_1=1\) and \(p_2=1.05\), and utility is \(u(c_1,c_2)=c_1^{0.5}c_2\).
Ex-2023-Q3.full_html: The interest rate changes from \(i=0.05\) to \(i'=1.84\). The graph's compensation slider is manual, so its labelled income and substitution effects are valid only after the compensated budget is set to the intended benchmark.
Ex-2023-Q3.answer_html:
Write lifetime wealth in period-2 value:

\[(1+i)p_1c_1+p_2c_2=(1+i)M_1+M_2.\]

For Cobb-Douglas exponents \(a=0.5\) and \(b=1\), expenditure shares are \(1/3\) and \(2/3\). Initially, lifetime wealth is \(215.25\), so

\[(c_1^0,c_2^0)=\left(\frac{1}{3}\frac{215.25}{1.05},\frac{2}{3}\frac{215.25}{1.05}\right)\approx(68.33,136.67).\]

After the interest-rate increase, lifetime wealth is \(403.2\) and the price of present consumption in future-value units is \(2.84\):

\[(c_1^1,c_2^1)\approx\left(\frac{1}{3}\frac{403.2}{2.84},\frac{2}{3}\frac{403.2}{1.05}\right)\approx(47.324,256).\]

The total effect on present consumption is negative. To decompose it, first choose the Hicksian or Slutsky benchmark and set the manual transfer so the compensated budget meets that condition; then substitution effect is compensated minus initial, and income effect is final minus compensated. Do not report the arrows before calibrating that transfer.

IE-SE-CobbDouglas.card_intro: Decompose a price change under Cobb-Douglas preferences into substitution and income effects.
IE-SE-CobbDouglas.card_prompt: Change the price, set the compensation benchmark and verify that the two component movements add to the total effect.
IE-SE-CobbDouglas.intro_html: A price change both alters relative prices and changes purchasing power. The compensated bundle isolates the relative-price response; the movement from that compensated bundle to the final Marshallian choice captures the income effect.
IE-SE-CobbDouglas.full_html:
For a rise in the price of good \(y\), the Hicksian substitution effect reduces compensated demand for \(y\). Because both Cobb-Douglas goods are normal, the loss of real income also reduces demand for \(y\), so the two effects reinforce each other.

For good \(x\), Marshallian demand in the graph is \(x^{*}=I/(2p_x)\) and therefore does not change when only \(p_y\) rises. Its positive substitution effect is exactly offset by its negative income effect.

Using bundle notation,

\[y^1-y^0=(y^c-y^0)+(y^1-y^c).\]

The first term is the substitution effect and the second is the income effect. The graph’s active compensation formula sets the transfer equal to Hicksian compensating variation, so the compensated bundle holds original utility fixed. A Slutsky decomposition would instead require enough income to make the original bundle affordable at new prices.

IE-SE-Quasilinear.display_title: Income and Substitution Effects: Quasilinear Utility
IE-SE-Quasilinear.card_intro: See how quasilinear demand changes the balance between substitution and income effects after a tax on good 1.
IE-SE-Quasilinear.card_prompt: Adjust the compensation correctly, then compare the decompositions for x and y.
IE-SE-Quasilinear.intro_html: The graph uses \(u(x,y)=x+\sqrt y\). A unit tax on good 1 raises its effective price from \(p_1\) to \(p_1+t_1\).
IE-SE-Quasilinear.full_html:
At an interior solution, the Marshallian demands are

\[y^{*}=\left(\frac{p_1}{2p_2}\right)^2,\qquad x^{*}=\frac{I}{p_1}-\frac{p_1}{4p_2}.\]

Demand for \(y\) does not depend on income at the interior solution, so its income effect is zero: its response to the relative-price change is entirely a substitution effect. Good \(x\) absorbs marginal income and therefore carries the income adjustment.

The graph's effect arrows depend on a manual compensation parameter. Set that transfer to the chosen Hicksian or Slutsky benchmark before interpreting the decomposition; otherwise the displayed components need not sum to the economically intended comparison.

Intertemporal-consumption.card_intro: Treat present and future consumption as two goods linked by the interest rate and lifetime resources.
Intertemporal-consumption.card_prompt: Change the interest rate and endowments, then identify whether the consumer is a borrower or a saver.
Intertemporal-consumption.intro_html:
The intertemporal budget constraint converts resources from the two periods into a common value. In future-value form,

\[(1+i)p_1c_1+p_2c_2=(1+i)M_1+M_2.\]
Intertemporal-consumption.full_html:
The endowment or zero-saving bundle is \((M_1/p_1,M_2/p_2)\). Choosing present consumption above the first coordinate requires borrowing; choosing less implies saving. The budget-line slope has magnitude \((1+i)p_1/p_2\), the market trade-off between present and future consumption.

At a smooth interior optimum, the marginal rate of time preference equals that market trade-off. A higher interest rate rotates the budget line around the endowment point: present consumption becomes more expensive in future-consumption units. The substitution effect therefore favours future consumption, while the income effect depends on whether the person is initially a saver or borrower.

Time-IE-SE.card_intro: Decompose the response to an interest-rate change for several intertemporal preference types.
Time-IE-SE.card_prompt: Select a utility type, identify borrower or saver status and compare the Hicksian decomposition after the interest-rate change.
Time-IE-SE.intro_html: An interest-rate change rotates the intertemporal budget line around the zero-saving endowment bundle. The graph compares Cobb-Douglas, perfect-complements and perfect-substitutes cases and provides a manual compensated budget.
Time-IE-SE.full_html:
When the interest rate rises, present consumption becomes relatively more expensive in future-value terms. The compensated substitution effect therefore moves away from present consumption whenever a smooth substitution response exists. The income effect is not universal: a saver benefits from a higher return, while a borrower faces a higher repayment cost. The total change can therefore differ across endowments and preferences.

Kinks and corners also matter. Perfect complements have a zero Hicksian substitution effect because the compensated bundle remains at the same kink. Perfect substitutes can jump between corners. The active graph formulas set compensation equal to each utility type’s Hicksian compensating variation. If those links are replaced by manual transfer values, recalibrate them before interpreting the arrows.

Consumer-Optimization.card_intro: Connect the budget line and utility maximisation to demand, price-consumption and income-consumption curves.
Consumer-Optimization.card_prompt: Change one price or income at a time and trace how the optimal bundle generates the corresponding demand relationship.
Consumer-Optimization.intro_html: This graph is a compact consumer-optimisation laboratory. It displays the budget line, utility representation, demand functions and optimum, then traces the paths created by repeated price or income changes.
Consumer-Optimization.full_html:
At a smooth interior optimum, \(MRS=p_x/p_y\) and the budget binds. A price change rotates the budget line and traces a price-consumption curve; projecting the chosen quantity against that price gives ordinary demand. An income change shifts the budget line in parallel and traces an income-consumption curve; projecting quantity against income gives an Engel curve.

Use the panels as linked views of the same optimisation problem. If a formula predicts an interior choice outside the feasible set, return to the original problem and check corners or kinks rather than forcing the tangency condition.
